did_you_know.text: Isaiah mentions Bel and Nebo as false idols that have collapsed, and describes their images as burdens loaded onto animals instead of being able to save anyone themselves.
The images do not merely collapse; according to the verse, they are also carried away into captivity and are unable to rescue the burden placed on them.
The chapter’s central contrast is between idols carried by animals and the Lord, who carries the house of Jacob: Israel is described as being carried by the Lord from birth, from the womb.

The Lord promises to continue carrying Israel even in old age and gray hairs. The sequence of verbs—“I have made,” “I will carry,” “I will sustain,” and “I will rescue”—emphasizes His ongoing responsibility for His people.

The question “To whom will you compare me?” emphasizes that the Lord cannot be compared to an idol or to an image made by human hands; the attempt to compare them lies at the heart of the argument against idolatry.
The making of an idol is described as a human and financially funded process: people weigh out gold and silver, hire a metalworker, and he makes a god from them.
After those who serve the idol carry it and set it in place, it remains there and cannot move; even if they call to it, it will not answer or save them from trouble.
The chapter calls the transgressors to “take it to heart” and remember—that is, to come to their senses and reconsider their actions and the difference between the Lord and the idols.
The Lord presents Himself as the only God: “I am God, and there is no other.” The claim is not merely that no idol is worthy of worship, but that there is no other God equal to Him.

The Lord’s uniqueness is described by the fact that He declares the end from the beginning and carries out His plan. He later mentions a man from a distant land, coming from the east, as part of the fulfillment of His purpose.
